Microwave techniques are as old as the early days of radio.
DISCUSSION
Although microwave has been around for a long time, there was little use for high frequency microwave signals.
Signals in the frequency range of 950 to 1600 kHz (AM radio band) was all that were needed for communications.
Radio transmission progressed into the microwave region early during World War II.
Using these high frequency microwave signals, a system called RADAR, Radio Detection and Ranging, was developed. A use for microwave was found.
RADAR allowed detection of enemy airplanes and ships and accurately determined their position.
As with many other wartime inventions, microwave techniques found their way into civilian applications such as air traffic control systems.
Today, microwave is not only used in RADAR systems, but is replacing telephone and telegraph wires and poles.
Microwave technology expanded into communications.
In fact, microwave is used more and more each day. As the need for communications increase, the need for higher frequencies also increase.
You can see by the frequency spectrum below how many frequency ranges are already being used. This shows the demand for more channels.
The frequency spectrum starts at zero hertz and increases to some value far beyond our hearing or sight capabilities.
The audio band, frequencies that you can hear, starts at 20 Hz and extends to approximately 20 kHz.
Most telephone communications occur in the audio band.
With the invention of radio, additional frequencies were needed. The band of frequencies between 950 kHz and 1600 kHz was designated the AM Radio band.
As the demand for frequencies increased, a new band was added to the spectrum. Short Wave radio was designated from 1600 kHz to 20 MHz.
When television and FM radio were introduced, additional frequencies in the radio spectrum had to be added. This band is called VHF or Very High Frequency.
When the VHF band was allocated, nobody believed that there would be a need for more than 13 channels! This was not the case and the UHF (Ultra High Frequency) band was added.
With a greater demand for radio frequencies, the microwave band was added to the frequency spectrum.
The microwave band ranges between 1 and 40 GHz.
Looking at the entire frequency spectrum, you can see that there are many bands, with each one including its own large range of frequencies.in each band.
To prevent overlapping of transmitted signals, there are certain frequencies in each band that are not used.
For example, in the AM band, each station is assigned a frequency range in which to operate, called a channel.
On each side of the assigned channel is an area called a guard band. No transmission is allowed in this area.
The guard bands keep one AM station from interfering with another AM station.
The microwave band operates in the same way. Channels and guard bands are assigned to prevent interference.
The microwave system used in this course operates at a frequency of 10.5 GHz. Notice that it is the middle of a channel with guard bands on each side.

To this point we have talked primarily about the carrier frequencies. Carrier frequencies convey no information.
Amplitude Modulation (AM) and Frequency Modulation (FM) are two common modulation techniques. modulated for example.
Once the carrier has been modulated, the microwave signal contains information.
Information, like everthing else in this world, requires a certain amount of space. space.
The space available for information, or modulation, must not interfere with the guard bands. Information is limited to a certain bandwidth.
For example, if a channel is assigned a bandwidth of 12 MHz, the modulation is contained within 6 MHz of the carrier frequency.
If the carrier frequency is 10.494 GHz, the lower limit of the bandwidth is 10.404 GHz and the upper limit of the bandwidth is 10.506 GHz.
To use another example, when the maximum modulation of the information is 10 MHz, the bandwidth must be 20 MHz (2 times the maximum modulation).
If the bandwidth is 8 MHz, what is the largest modulation signal allowed?
8 MHz is the bandwidth. Remember, the maximum modulation signal is equal to 1/2 of the bandwidth.

The radio frequencies when transmitted are often referred to as electromagnetic waves.
These electromagnetic waves travel from one point to another differently depending on their frequency.
The three ways the electromagnetic waves travel are: ound Waves Sky Waves Direct Waves
Ground waves are signals that have long wavelengths and tend to follow the curvature of the earth.
Frequencies below 1600 kHz are transmitted from the antenna as ground waves.
The range of ground waves is several hundred miles and is limited by the type of terrain and any obstructions such as mountains or buildings.
At higher frequencies, sky waves are used instead of ground waves..
Sky waves occur mainly in frequencies from 1600 kHz to 30 MHz. The transmitted RF is radiated toward the sky at an angle.
The RF energy is reflected back to the earth's surface by the ionosphere layer of the atmosphere. However, some signals are not reflected back.
Sky waves are short wave communications signals that are able to travel long distances..
At even higher frequencies, the RF energy starts to behave as light.
Direct waves occur in the UHF and microwave region, 30 MHz to 100 GHz. The RF energy travels in a straight line or line of sight.
The distance that direct waves travel is limited by the curvature of the earth. For long distance transmission, repeater stations are used.
The ground, sky and direct waves transmit overlapping frequencies. The table below indicates where each type of wave has the greatest effect.
Microwave has advantages and disadvantages over the other frequency bands.
The main advantages of microwave is the small component size and the high directivity of the signal.
Small component size is due to the wavelength of microwave.
To operate efficiently, many microwave component dimensions are manufactured at either 1, 1/2 or 1/4 wavelength. This allows for very small component dimensions.
High directivity, due to most microwave being direct waves, allows all the transmitted power to be directed in one direction.
This prevents loss due to the RF energy being scattered in all directions.
Main disadvantages of the microwave are high component cost, short range and the attenuating effect of weather.
High component cost is due to the manufacturing process, which is more difficult because of the small size of components required.
The short range is due to the direct waves. Long distance transmission requires repeater stations.
The attenuating effect of weather is due to microwave behaving as light.
For example, on a clear night an automobile's headlights can illuminate long distances.
On a foggy night, the headlight's illumination decreases. Light is attenuated by the fog..
Even with the disadvantages of microwave frequencies, microwave is used more and more as the need for radar and communications systems increases.

METRIC PREFIXES REVIEW

There must be a unit of measure and a value in all electronic measurements. For example: Units of Measure Values Frequency..................Hertz Resistance.................Ohms Current....................Amperes Voltage....................Volts
Units of Measure Values Frequency.......................Hertz Resistance.....................Ohms Current............................Amperes Voltage............................Volts
DISCUSSION

Some of these values are very large or very small. Metric prefixes are used so that a lot of zeroes are not needed. alues Prefixes 1,000,000 Hertz is 1 MHz 15,000 Ohms is 15 k .001 Amperes is 1 mA .000015 Volts is 15 V

The table below shows the decimal number, the equivalent power of ten, the metric prefix and the symbol. Numbers Powers of Ten Prefix Symbol 1 10 unit 1,000 10 kilo k 1,000,000 10 mega M 1,000,000,000 10 giga G
The table now shows the values and prefixes for numbers less than 1. .001 10 milli m .000001 micro .000000001 nano n
There are other metric prefixes, but these are not used very often in electronics. 10 10 ff d .01 10 centi c 100000000000 10 Tera T .000000000000001 10 femto f
Placing metric prefixes on a linear scale gives a graphic representation of how they are related.
Changing numbers between decimal and metric prefixes is easy when the linear scale is used. Let's see.
To change 8,000 to a metric value, place 8,000 on the scale. ga Mega kilo Units milli micro nano 8 0 0 0 9 6 3 0 -3 -6 -9 10 10 10 10 10 10 10
In numbers greater than 1 like 8,000, it is understood that a decimal point will be to the right of the whole number.
To change 8,000 to a metric value, move the decimal to the left three places. 8,000 is 8 kilo or 8 k.

To change a metric value to units, place the metric number on the scale. 9.5 M is placed as shown. Note the position of the decimal point. Giga Mega kilo Units milli micro nano 9 5 9 6 3 0 -3 -6 -9 10 10 10 10 10 10 10
Move the decimal point six places to the right. 9.5 M is 9,500,000 units.
Numbers less than 1 are converted the same way, only the decimal point is moved in the opposite direction. Let's see. Giga Mega kilo Units milli micro nano 9 6 3 0 -3 -6 -9 10 10 10 10 10 10 10
To change .008 to a metric value, place .008 on the scale. ga Mega kilo Units milli micro nano 0 0 8 9 6 3 0 -3 -6 -9 10 10 10 10 10 10 10
In numbers less than 1 like .008, it is understood that a decimal point will be to the left of the whole number.
To change .008 to a metric value, move the decimal to the right three places. .008 is 8 milli or 8 m.

To change a metric value to units, place the metric number on the scale. 9.5 m is placed as shown. Note the position of the decimal point. ga Mega kilo Units milli micro nano 9 5 9 6 3 0 -3 -6 -9 10 10 10 10 10 10 10
Move the decimal point six places to the left. 9.5 m is .0000095 units.
